added_provisions.reason: The map recorded paragraphs (a), (c) and (d) of rule (20) of section 31 but not paragraph (b), which is the attestation paragraph that turns on the witnesses: the notary must state whether he knows the executants himself or whether the witnesses know them, and in the latter case which executant each witness knows. It is the attestation counterpart of the identification limb of rule (9) on which this matter turns. It is added as a supporting provision with applicable_to_matter_date false, because Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11)(a) repealed the earlier paragraph (b) without setting it out, so the corpus holds only the post-2022 wording.

question_decisions.note: The authority requirement is confirmed. The precautions asked about are laid down expressly in section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance and in sections 7 and 10 to 13 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, and no judicial authority is needed to list them; a search of the corpus turned up no other Act governing witnesses to a notarially executed will, and the Wills Ordinance No. 21 of 1844 contains no witness provision at all. The status is downgraded for two reasons. First, the ground on which the answer refuses the nurse rests on a reading of rule (9) that the October 2018 wording does not clearly bear, and on rule (20)(c), which requires the witnesses' own names and residences rather than their knowledge of the testator. Second, completeness cannot be established from the corpus: rule (10) of section 31 was in force at the matter date and is not reproduced anywhere, and the pre-2022 wording of rule (20)(b) is lost in the same way, so a question asking what precautions to take about witnesses cannot be answered exhaustively from the corpus text.

disagreements.researcher_position: The nurse should be refused as a witness because she cannot make the declaration of acquaintance contemplated by rule (9) and cannot supply from her own knowledge the particulars of the testator that rule (20)(c) requires the attestation to carry, even though the Notary's own knowledge of the testator meets the identification limb of rule (9).
disagreements.verifier_position: On the October 2018 wording the vetting and declaration duty in rule (9) was introduced by the words 'and in the latter case', so it applied where the notary relied on the attesting witnesses' knowledge of the executant. This Notary knows the testator, so the corpus does not show that duty to be owed on these facts, and rule (20)(c) supplies no independent ground because it calls for the full names and residences of the attesting witnesses themselves. Refusing the nurse is sound practice and may well be what the pre-2022 rule (20)(b) required, but the corpus as it stands does not carry it as a duty.

disagreements.researcher_position: Rule (10) is recorded as a corpus gap, but the answer is still put forward as proposed gold.
disagreements.verifier_position: Rule (10) sat between the identification rule (9) and the reading-over rule (11) and was repealed only in 2024 without being reproduced; the pre-2022 wording of rule (20)(b), the witness-facing attestation paragraph, is lost in the same way. A gold answer to a question that asks for the precautions relating to witnesses should not be fixed until a 2018 print of the Ordinance is consulted.

unsupported_claims: CL-M100-Q01-013: the stated grounds for refusing the nurse are not carried by the provisions cited. Rule (9)'s vetting and declaration duty attached at the matter date to the case where the notary relied on the witnesses' knowledge of the executant, and this Notary knows the testator; rule (20)(c) requires the witnesses' own full names and residences, not their knowledge of the testator. Marked disputed.
CL-M100-Q01-017: the conclusion is otherwise well supported, but the limb refusing the nurse inherits the same difficulty. Marked disputed.
All fifteen other claims are supported by the provisions cited and by facts in the enriched background, and are marked verified.
temporal_issues: Rule (10) of section 31 was in force in October 2018 and was repealed by Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(4) without being reproduced. Its content is unrecoverable from the corpus and it sat among the witness and identification rules.

The pre-2022 wording of rule (20)(b) of section 31, the only attestation paragraph that turns on the witnesses' knowledge of the executant, was repealed and replaced by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11)(a) without being set out. Recorded as PROV-M100-901.

The temporal note on PROV-M100-008 cites section 34(1)(b) in its post-2022 form; Act No. 31 of 2022 s.17 substituted the whole of section 34, so the October 2018 penalty for a breach of rule (11) is not in the corpus. Provision marked partially_verified.

Rule (20)(h), which requires the attestation of a will to state that the testator was of good and sound mind, was inserted only by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11)(d). The researcher rightly did not rely on it despite the background about the testator's mind, and it must not be used at this matter date.

PROV-M100-014 (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.4) and PROV-M100-016 (rule (14)) are correctly flagged applicable_to_matter_date false; Act No. 30 of 2022 s.3(2) and Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(7) each replace without reproducing, so the 2018 wording is lost in both cases.

Rule numbering is stable across the period: Act No. 47 of 2011 s.3 renumbers only within rule (26), and Act No. 20 of 1976 s.10 touches only rules (29) and (36), so the rule numbers used in the map are the numbers in force in October 2018.
missing_definitions_or_exceptions: Rule (20)(b) was missing from the map and has been added as PROV-M100-901.
Neither Ordinance defines 'witness' or 'attesting witness'; defs on 1-1907 and 7-1840 return nothing, so the researcher's statement that no defined term bears on the answer holds.

Rule (15) of section 31, on signatures made with a mark or in a language other than that in which the notary practises, is an exception the map does not record. It does not change the answer, because rule (8) requires at least two witnesses subscribing in letters, but it is worth noting for the case where a proposed witness can only make a mark.

Rule (36)(c) of section 31, excusing a non-attorney notary's attendance at his office where the signatory is believed to be on the point of death, is the only provision bearing on a bedside execution; the researcher correctly treated it as not a witness rule.

Section 44 of the Registration of Title Act No. 21 of 1998 and sections 4 and 5 of the Deeds and Documents (Execution before Public Officers) Ordinance No. 17 of 1852 use similar language about attesting witnesses, but neither governs a will executed before a notary, so neither is a missed alternative.
case_law_dependence: The answer cites no case law, and none is needed to list the statutory precautions.

Witness competency as such (age, blindness, deafness, illiteracy, relationship short of taking a benefit) is not in the corpus. Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.10 presupposes a law of competency without stating it, so an answer that went beyond the statutory precautions would need judicial authority. The gold answer does not go there, which is why the authority requirement stays statute_only.
enrichment_issues: No statute name, section number or rule number appears in the enriched background, and the conclusion is not stated in it.

The enrichment does pre-sort the candidates: it says of the two neighbours that each knows the testator's proper name, occupation and residence, takes nothing under the Will, is not married to anyone who takes under it, and can sign in letters. Those are the elements of rule (8), rule (9) and Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.11 restated as facts, so a model could pick the right witnesses without knowing the rules. The facts are legitimate, but the question tests less than it appears to.
Every synthetic_decisive fact (FACT-M100-Q01-003, -004, -005) states why it is needed and what would change without it, and none changes the legal issue.
duplicate_or_leak_issues: No provision is recorded twice; the twelve entries drawn from 1-1907/s31 are distinct rules or paragraphs.

CL-M100-Q01-013 carries the fact id 'BG-1', which is not declared in the enrichment block and does not match the FACT-M100-Qnn-nnn pattern. It appears to mean the original background fact that the Notary knows the testator. Left as written, but it should be normalized before the set is published.

lawyer_questions: In October 2018, when rule (9) of section 31 still read 'unless the person executing the same be known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses thereto; and in the latter case, he shall satisfy himself...', did the duty to vet the witnesses and to take their signed declaration of acquaintance apply where the notary himself knew the testator? That decides whether this Notary may accept the nurse and whether the declaration at the foot of the Will was then obligatory.
What did rule (10) of section 31 provide before its repeal by Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(4), and did it bear on the witnesses?
What was the wording of paragraph (b) of rule (20) of section 31 before Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(11)(a) replaced it, and did it require the notary to state which executant each witness knew?

Does anything outside the corpus govern the competency of an attesting witness to a will (age, blindness, deafness, illiteracy, relationship to the testator), given that Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.10 assumes such a law without stating it?
